definition: Coerce means to force someone to act through threats or pressure.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word coerce. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know coerce should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The loan shark coerced shop owners into paying 'protection' fees by hinting at what happened to stores that refused.
A nudge is far gentler than coercing — a hint, a reminder, a little push that leaves the choice entirely free.
Arm-twisting is milder than coercing — heavy, insistent pressure, but still short of the open threats that make refusal feel dangerous.

To compel is to force by any means, including bare circumstance — an empty fuel tank can compel a change of plans, with no one threatening anyone. Coerce always needs a person applying the pressure: the yes is manufactured through threats or fear, which is why the word accuses.

To browbeat is to bully someone face to face — words, glares, and repetition until they give in. Coerce is broader and darker: the pressure runs through threats of real harm, not just an overbearing manner, and it can be applied from a distance.
to win agreement freely, with reasons
to tempt someone gently and patiently toward a choice

Coerce means to force someone to act through threats or pressure.
The team captain coerced the younger players into 'volunteering' for his extra laps — anyone who said no found his gear missing on match day.
Coerce is stronger than 'pressure' and different from 'persuade': persuasion wins a free yes, while coercion manufactures a yes through fear.
The moment agreement is given freely, it is no longer coercion.
Coerce is the word courts and reporters use when a yes was manufactured by fear — it always implies wrongdoing.
'Pressure' is the everyday cousin; 'force' covers physical compulsion too.
Coerce names the act; its unit-mate duress names the unlawful pressure the victim was under — you coerce someone, who then acts under duress.

In the mill towns of the 1880s, Election Day began at the factory gate.
Owners rarely needed to say much.
Foremen handed out ballots already marked, and the men who took them understood what refusing might cost.
Historians argue about how often owners had to coerce their workers outright — docking wages, threatening the company houses their families slept in.
Often the threat never needed saying twice.
One eviction in October was enough to settle a hundred votes in November.
Reformers pushed for the secret ballot for exactly this reason: a vote no one can see is a vote no one can punish.
